finding.claim: load_user takes caller identity from the client-controlled X-Session-User-Verified header with no verification, so any caller can impersonate any user with grants on a file and delete (views.py:18) or rename (views.py:27) it.
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') at views.py:17 gating delete at views.py:18; is_allowed(g.user, f, 'write') at views.py:25 gating rename at views.py:27

trace.note: before_request load_user runs on every request
g.user set directly from request header, no signature/session check
DELETE handler calls ensure_allowed with g.user
is_allowed looks up grants[g.user]; attacker-chosen name selects which grants apply
abort(403) only when the forged user lacks the action
rename path uses the same forged g.user

finding.guards_checked: ACL checks at acl.py:4-10 and views.py:25 are correct and gate their actions; None user (header absent) yields 403. No check validates the identity header. Exploitability depends on deployment: a trusted proxy that strips and sets X-Session-User-Verified would mitigate, and this is not visible in the code.

verdict.guard_found: Only ACL checks exist, and they test authorization for whatever identity is supplied, not the identity itself. ensure_allowed at views.py:17 is a bare call, but it raises via abort(403) at acl.py:10, so the delete is not reached on failure. is_allowed at views.py:25 is tested with `not`, so the rename is gated the same way. Nothing validates X-Session-User-Verified: load_user at views.py:11 copies it straight into g.user. A missing header gives None, which yields no grants and a 403 (acl.py:5).
verdict.reason: load_user at views.py:11 sets g.user from the request header with no verification, and the ACL checks at acl.py:5-10 and views.py:17 and 25 only authorize whatever name the client supplies, so any unauthenticated caller can delete (views.py:18) or rename (views.py:27) a file by naming a user who holds the grant. The only mitigation is a trusted proxy that strips and sets this header, which is not visible in this code, so the finding stands for the code as written and should be flagged as deployment-dependent.

finding.claim: Grant check uses substring membership, so if a user's grants are stored as a string rather than a list, action 'write' matches grants like 'rewrite' and similar partial matches.
finding.source: action argument and stored grants[user] value (data shape not visible in code)
finding.sink: 'action in resource.get("grants", {}).get(user, [])' at acl.py:5, consumed by views.py:17 and views.py:25

trace.note: membership test on whatever grants[user] holds

finding.guards_checked: Default [] is a list, which gives exact-match semantics. Only a string-valued grants entry triggers substring matching. Candidate only; storage format is not in the audited code.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts with 403 when is_allowed is False and its result is not discarded, and rename_file (views.py:25-26) tests the return value. Neither control stops substring matching inside is_allowed (acl.py:5). The substring behaviour exists only if grants[user] is a string, and no code in the repo writes to STORE or sets grants, so the storage shape is not visible.
verdict.reason: The trace lines exist and are accurately described, but acl.py:5 uses list-membership semantics for the code shown, and substring matching happens only if the unseen stored grants value is a string, which the repo never populates (STORE = {} at views.py:6, no writes). The attacker-side reachability also depends on X-Session-User-Verified (views.py:11), a client-supplied header, which is set outside this code, so this cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: Missing file ids raise KeyError (500) before the ACL check runs, while existing but unauthorized ids return 403. Status codes let a caller enumerate which file ids exist.
finding.sink: STORE[fid] lookup at views.py:16 and views.py:24, before ensure_allowed/is_allowed

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for unknown id, yielding 500
ensure_allowed runs only for existing ids

finding.guards_checked: No existence check or uniform error response before the ACL check. Low severity: enumeration only, no authorization bypass.

verdict.guard_found: none before the lookup. views.py:16 and views.py:24 index STORE[fid] directly with no existence check and no try/except, and no error handler is defined in views.py. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) and is_allowed (views.py:25) run only after the lookup succeeds.
verdict.reason: A missing id raises an unhandled KeyError at views.py:16 (or :24), which Flask returns as a 500, while an existing id that fails the check returns 403 via abort(403) at acl.py:10 (or views.py:26), so any caller who can reach the endpoint can tell which ids exist; the attacker needs no role beyond sending a request, and the impact is enumeration only, consistent with the candidate's low severity.
